newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Hong Kong interim body may breach Basic Law - UK.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong interim body may breach Basic Law - UK.

text.p: Britain's Foreign Secretary said on Thursday China's move to set up a provisonal legislature to help rule Hong Kong after it takes over the colony could be a severe breach of earlier Chinese promises.

Malcolm Rifkind reiterated in an interview with Reuters Television that he would like to refer the issue to the International Court of Justice (ICJ or the world court), but added he was not optimistic that Beijing would allow this.
Rifkind was due to meet Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen in Singapore on Friday on the fringes of the Asia-Europe meeting, a gathering of foreign ministers from 25 countries.
He said the talks with Qian would focus on Hong Kong and Chinese proposals to change the territory's laws.
Britain hands back Hong Kong to China at midnight on June 30 after more than 150 years of colonial rule.
The terms of the handover were laid out under a Sino-British joint declaration in 1984, the main points of which were put into Hong Kong's Basic Law, announced by China in 1990.
But Britain says China has broken promises it made over Hong Kong by setting up a provisional legislature of pro-Beijing personalities to set laws for the territory after the handover.
"We believe the establishment of the provisional legislature certainly goes against the spirit and indeed may be a severe breach of the joint declaration and the Basic Law," Rifkind said.

"One way of resolving this would be to allow the International Court of Justice to address these matters. We would be happy to do that but the ICJ can only look at these issues if both sides of the dispute agree," he said.
"Up till now the Chinese, perhaps not surprisingly, have declined to allow the matter to go for that kind of judgment."
Asked if he thought Beijing would change its mind, and allow the issue to go to the world court, Rifkind replied:
"I am not wildly optimistic. It may be because they are not convinced of the strength of their position."

Rifkind said he was not been surprised by the setting up of the provisional legislature or the proposal to repeal some parts of laws affecting civil liberties in Hong Kong, including parts of its Bill of Rights.
But he said the moves would hurt Hong Kong.
"It is important in a constructive way that Britain and China address these issues and see what prospects there are for some amelioration and a resolution of this particular difficulty," he said.

"It is certainly crucial China understands that the prosperity and the extraordinary economic success of Hong Kong cannot be divorced from the Hong Kong way of life and half of that Hong Kong way of life is that Hong Kong has had a free society," he said.

"The rule of law has been supreme. People have enjoyed a wide range of basic political rights. Any diminution of these rights will not just be highly regrettable in itself. It will also have significant consequences for the confidence in the territory and for its economic success."
